World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Breaking: Large fire reported at oil refinery in Geelong
World.content:
A fire has broken out at one of Australia's two currently operational oil refineries, with residents in parts of Geelong told to stay indoors due to smoke.

Victoria Police has told the ABC emergency services were called to reports of a large fire at the Corio refinery around 11pm.

People in the area have been asked to stay indoors and close their windows due to the large amount of smoke in the area.

Fire and Rescue Victoria has been contacted for comment.

The Country Fire Authority issued a watch and act for a large swathe of Geelong, with the warning urging "anyone located in to the south of Refinery Road Corio" to take shelter indoors immediately.

"There is a factory fire in Refinery Road, Corio," the advice said.

"A wind change has caused the smoke to be blown towards the Northern Geelong area."

Residents were also being urged to keep off the roads to allow emergency services to respond.

The Victoria Emergency website shows a large blaze reported on Refinery Rd, Corio, which is not yet under control.

The incident map said 10 vehicles were responding to the blaze.

World.title: Boy kills students and teacher in school shooting in Türkiye
World.content:
At least nine people, including eight children, have been killed in a school shooting in Türkiye - the country's second school attack in two days.

A boy, believed to be aged 13 or 14, carried out the shooting in southeastern Türkiye on Wednesday, killing his fellow students and a teacher.

At least 13 other students have been injured in the attack.

The governor of Kahramanmaras, Mukerrem Unluer, said the shooter arrived at his school carrying five guns and seven magazines.

"An eighth-grade student... came to school with guns that we believe belonged to his father in his backpack," he said.

"He entered two classrooms and opened fire randomly, causing injuries and deaths."

The governor said that was before he shot and killed himself.

Eighth-grade students in Türkiye are usually aged 13 or 14.

The student shooter was the son of a former police officer, according to Mr Unluer.

Local Turkish media has reported that the student's father has been detained.

"We suspect he may have taken his father's weapons," the governor said.

Police and paramedics have surrounded the school, while the country's justice minister said prosecutors had launched an immediate investigation.

Videos of the scene show students jumping out of windows and fleeing the school grounds through a courtyard.

About 15 gunshots can be heard in the one-and-a-half-minute video.

Turkish security forces and emergency staff outside the high school where a shooting took place on Tuesday. (Mevlut Bayraktar/IHA via AP)

School shootings were rare in Türkiye, but this is the second school shooting in two days.

On Tuesday, a former student opened fire at a school in the southeastern province of Sanliurfa, injuring at least 16 people, including students and teachers, before killing himself.

Reuters/AFP

World.title: American YouTuber jailed in South Korea for being a public nuisance
World.content:
An American YouTuber has been jailed in South Korea for being a public nuisance after he filmed himself kissing a statue commemorating Korean war sex slaves.

Johnny Somali was sentenced to six months in prison for displaying “severe” disrespect for South Korean law.

The 25-year-old has gained notoriety for recording himself doing several provocative stunts in South Korea and Japan and streaming them on platforms including YouTube and Twitch.

The Seoul Western District Court found Somali, whose real name is Ramsey Khalid Ismael, guilty of offences including violating the Minor Offences Act which covers a wide variety of public order crimes, obstruction of business and distribution of false video content.

Prosecutors had sought a three year jail sentence for the self-confessed "internet troll" who was also accused of harassing staff and visitors at an amusement park, disrupting a convenience store by blasting North Korean music and tipping over a cup of noodles onto a table.

Comfort women court order A South Korean court orders Japan to financially compensate 12 South Korean women forced to work as sex slaves for Japanese troops during World War II in a landmark ruling.

He also caused similar disruption on a bus and subway and distributed non-consensual deepfake videos.

The court ordered Somali's immediate detention following the verdict, believing he was a flight risk.

The live streamer caused public outrage in South Korea after he uploaded a video of himself kissing and twerking beside a statue memorialising Korean 'comfort women', a term used for women forced into sexual slavery by Japanese occupying forces before and during World War II.

The clip was later removed.

Somali apologised at the time of his indictment, saying he was "not aware of the significance of the statue".

"I am remorseful," he said again on his way into court on Wednesday.

"I want to apologise to the people of Korea.

"And I want to change my life and become a better person."

Somali's viral internet following came about after he engaged in disruptive acts, including spilling cup noodle soup on a table at a Seoul convenience store and playing loud North Korean music in public.

In 2023, Somali caused annoyance in Japan for taunting subway commuters about Nagasaki and Hiroshima, the two cities devastated by United States' atomic bombs in 1945.

AFP/AP

World.title: Defence spending to climb by $53 billion as 'international norms' erode
World.content:
Australia's defence spending will climb by $53 billion over the next decade as the federal government says it responds to "intensifying" global risks.

That injection includes a $14 billion lift in spending over the next four years.

The federal government will tomorrow release the 2026 National Defence Strategy (NDS), which aims to map out both the strategic landscape Australia is facing and the capabilities defence will require to meet those future challenges.

The government claims the new funding will take Australian defence spending to roughly 3 per cent of GDP by 2033 when measured using NATO's methodology, which includes defence-adjacent spending in areas like pensions.

The last NDS, released in 2024, warned of increasing strategic competition between the United States and China and of an unprecedented military build-up in the Indo-Pacific.

Recent conflicts have also had a heavy influence on the new strategy, particularly the conflict in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine.

Australia faces the most threatening strategic circumstances since World War II, according to the defence minister. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

In a speech to be delivered tomorrow, excerpts of which have been provided to the ABC, Defence Minister Richard Marles will say those trends identified in 2024 are only worsening.

"[The strategy] affirms that Australia faces its most complex and threatening strategic circumstances since the end of World War II," the excerpts read.

"International norms that once constrained the use of force and military coercion continue to erode.

"More countries are engaged in conflict today than at any time since the end of World War II, and this is occurring across every region of the world.

"In the face of this, the Albanese Government is pursuing every avenue of increasing defence capability quickly: mostly through bigger defence appropriations but also through accessing private capital."

Building a bigger budget

The $53 billion increase in spending takes into account some projects that have already been announced, including $12 billion towards the upgrade to the Henderson shipyards in Western Australia.

The facility will be used to dock and maintain nuclear-powered submarines under AUKUS and construct Mogami-class frigates in the future.

Government announces billions in spending on military drones Defence Minister Richard Marles says expanding Australia's fleet of autonomous and uncrewed systems will help keep the nation safe and boost Australia's sovereign defence industry.

It also includes between $2 billion and $5 billion on new investments into drone technology, as revealed earlier this week.

The bulk of the additional spending is due towards the back end of the coming decade, like $8.7 billion in 2033-34, and $9.8 billion in 2034-35.

The government has been under pressure from the US to lift its defence spending as a share of GDP, as it places similar pressure on other NATO allies.

At a meeting in Singapore last year, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told Mr Marles the US wanted to see a lift to 3.5 per cent of GDP.

Australian defence spending has typically been measured at roughly 2 per cent of GDP and forecast to rise to 2.33 per cent by 2033.

But the government has more recently argued that if Australia's defence bill is to be compared to other countries, NATO's methodology for measuring defence spending should be used.

Under that measurement — which includes some pensions for retired Australian Defence Force members, defence-related funding in other portfolios, housing subsidies for defence personnel and more — the government says defence spending as a share of GDP will climb from 2.8 per cent now, to 3 per cent in 2033.

'Reprioritisations' and 'alternative financing'

Not all of the increased spending will appear on government books when the budget is handed down next month.

The increased spending is expected to be partly funded through the sale of high-value defence real estate, as flagged last year.

But some will also come through what the government is calling "alternative financing", which might include taking equity stakes in companies or investing in government-business enterprises.

The government has also flagged "reprioritisations" within the plans to be released today, but details on what exactly is being axed, cut back or delayed are not yet known.

Iran war live updates: For the latest news on the Middle East crisis, read our blog

Mr Marles has said the decisions on axing or scaling back projects are "not easy", but necessary to free up funding for higher priorities.

Three years ago, the government significantly rolled back two army projects — slashing a planned acquisition of infantry fighting vehicles and rolling back planned orders for self-propelled Howitzers.

Any reprioritisations are likely to be politically contentious, with the Coalition arguing defence capabilities should not be cut back in one area to prioritise another.

World.title: Jury hears 'no bad blood' before sistergirl's alleged fatal stabbing
World.content:
A jury has heard a man accused of fatally stabbing a sistergirl from the Tiwi islands had "no bad blood" with the woman prior to witness accounts of him running towards her with a knife.

Andrew Mungatopi, 34, faced the first day of his trial in the Northern Territory Supreme Court after pleading not guilty to the murder of the sistergirl — who cannot be named for cultural reasons — in October 2024.

Mr Mungatopi pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of manslaughter — a plea the prosecution did not accept.

Sistergirl is a term used by some Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people to describe gender-diverse people who have a female spirit.

The unit in Fawcett Court in Darwin's northern suburbs where the incident happened. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

In his opening statement on Wednesday, Crown prosecutor Neil Kumar told the jury Mr Mungatopi had been staying at an apartment in Malak with the 37-year-old sistergirl and his partner and their child while visiting Darwin, along with a number of other people.

He said over the course of the trial — expected to run for two weeks — the jury would hear evidence from several children aged between 13 and 15 at the time who witnessed the incident.

Mr Kumar said a boy who referred to Mr Mungatopi as his uncle told police he saw the pair arguing over something someone said about Mr Mungatopi's partner, and that Mr Mungatopi had threatened the sistergirl.

He told the court a second child told police she saw Mr Mungatopi take a knife and stab the sistergirl.

The jury also heard a neighbour would testify to hearing someone repeatedly say: "I'm going to kill you, I'm going to kill you, I'm going to kill you."

Mr Kumar said a recording of a Triple Zero (000) call made by a neighbour after the incident would be played to the court, in which Mr Mungatopi said the sistergirl had been intoxicated and "ran into my knife" while he was cooking dinner.

The defence says the lack of animosity between the pair made the woman's death "jarring" and "so difficult to take". (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

In his opening statement, defence barrister Ambrith Abayasekara acknowledged that his client had accepted responsibility for causing the death of a family member and that there was "no excuse for what he did".

But Mr Abayasekara argued he could not be found guilty of murder as there was no intent to cause serious harm.

"What happened on the night of 7 October, 2024 was a family tragedy," he said.

"This was not a relationship where there was any pre-existing animosity, as there can be in some family relationships … there was no bad blood, no beef.

" This is why [the sistergirl's] death on that night is so jarring and so difficult to take. "

Mr Abayasekara said her death arose out of "nothing of any real consequence", in the context of people drinking.

He added that what Mr Mungatopi told police in the immediate aftermath was said during a time of "high trauma" and was not a "truthful account".

First witnesses give evidence

Tracey Burke, a close friend of the sistergirl, told the jury she was "shocked" to learn of her death as she had "never seen them argue."

Ms Burke said she had been at the apartment on the day of the alleged murder, drinking with the victim and other members of the family, until a disagreement arose after she tried to cut the victim off.

"I said 'you've reached your limit'," she said.

She said in response, the sistergirl had become aggressive and said: "I'll punch you in the face."

A witness told the court she heard Mr Mungatopi say "I'm going to stab you" on the night of the alleged murder. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Under cross-examination, Ms Burke said the sistergirl could "flip out" when she drank, though it never became physical.

"Most of the time we just laugh and get along … sometimes she doesn't know when to stop," she said.

" When alcohol gets involved, it gets tense with everybody. "

A second witness, Marlees Mungatopi — the sistergirl's aunt and owner of the apartment — testified that she had seen Mr Mungatopi drinking rum and cola from an emptied water bottle throughout the day and that he had become "very drunk".

Later that night, she said she saw him rush out the back door with an object before getting into a "scuffle" with the sistergirl, moving his arm towards her multiple times as she fell to the ground.

Under cross-examination, however, Marlees Mungatopi conceded Mr Mungatopi had not run but only "walked fast", and that she had not had a clear view of the sistergirl.

"Is it the case you were more drunk than you realise?" Mr Abayasekara asked, to which she replied "No, I wasn't."

The trial in the NT Supreme Court is expected to run for two weeks. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Marlees Mungatopi's daughter, Shanika Mungatopi, also testified.

She told the court she saw the sistergirl and Mr Mungatopi's partner arguing before he intervened and "slapped" the sistergirl in the face.

She said the sistergirl then walked outside to call police, at which point she saw Mr Mungatopi retrieve "a big sharp knife with a black handle" from the kitchen and run out after her.

"I seen him running," she said.

" He was saying — swearing at my missus … I'm going to stab you. "

Shanika Mungatopi is expected to face cross-examination when the trial continues in Darwin on Thursday.

World.title: Food minister warns of challenging times for WA consumers at checkout
World.content:
Food security and the price of groceries are set to only get more challenging, according to Western Australian Food and Agricultural Minister Jackie Jarvis.

She said there were real concerns around food supply with recent natural disasters on top of fuel and fertiliser supply issues and cost increases.

Speaking to the WA Country Hour, Ms Jarvis acknowledged food producers were facing tough business decisions amid rising input costs.

"It's inevitable that food prices are going to go up," she said.

"As we go through the season, decisions are going to have to be made about the cost of fuel and fertiliser versus the yield return you're going to get.

"We want to make sure that people are still planting crops."

Jackie Jarvis warns food will likely become more expensive. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Ms Jarvis said packaged food was not immune to the increase in prices, with freight costs also rising.

"Eighty per cent of our packaged food also comes across the Nullarbor, so we also have issues there," she said.

"That's also a concern."

Ms Jarvis said the dairy industry was already feeling the effects of higher operating costs.

"We have I think 99 or 100 dairy farmers in the state and I know they're really struggling with fuel prices, and they're going to be facing increased fertiliser charges," she said.

Last week, the WA government announced trucks would be able to take on an extra 10 tonnes of dairy and perishables to reduce transport costs.

The dairy industry has been hit by fuel and fertiliser costs. (ABC Rural: Annie Brown)

"It's a small thing, but it just means it provides some efficiency," Ms Jarvis said.

"We want the economy to keep ticking over and we are acutely aware that we need fresh food in this state.

" I think we are bracing ourselves for challenging times ahead. "

Carnarvon bananas 20 per cent more expensive

Carnarvon's Sweeter Banana Co-operative estimated about 90 per cent of this year's banana crop was damaged by Tropical Cyclone Narelle.

Doriana Mangili says every part of the supply chain has been affected by higher costs. (Supplied: Sweeter Banana Co-Operative)

Business manager Doriana Mangili said a lack of supply had resulted in prices increasing by 20 per cent, taking a bag of Carnarvon bananas from $4 to $6.

"Just in the last two months due to other world events, we've had every single supplier that supplies us advising us of increases in prices," she said.

Ms Mangili said every part of the supply chain was more expensive.

She said all farmers were experiencing a similar issue, and she only expected it to get worse.

"It's really serious beyond just bananas — there's a big, broader issue out there about food security," she said.

"How do we make sure that we have sustainable food prices that people can afford, given the climate of everything else that's going on beyond just our little cyclone?"

John Cummings says producers will inevitably pass on increasing costs to consumers. (Credit: Claire Moodie)

President of the WA Independent Growers Association John Cummings said supply contracts were locked in three to four months in advance so there was not an immediate impact.

However, he said this would change.

"Look, I think you'd be very naive to think that any manufacturer or builder or business in Australia was happy as the proverbial pig on the margins they're currently making," he said.

"They would be looking for every way they could to increase their prices and recover some of these extra costs, I don't think there's any doubt about that.

"It just takes a period of time and they've got to, each and every one of those businesses, have to walk a fine line of making sure that the price doesn't go up to a point where they're turning their customers off."

He said buyer consumption patterns had been changing for some time as prices increased and people were looking for cheaper options.

"There is far more mince being sold in supermarkets than there is cut meat," he said.

Mr Cummings said sales of chicken were higher as it was one of the cheapest forms of protein.

"So all those behavioural changes that consumers have made to save money over the last one to two years is probably going to get a bit wider as the cost of petrol and the cost of living cuts deeper," he said.

"We would expect them to continue, that rate of change that we've seen."

World.title: Coronial inquest finds death of sex offender at Corella Place was preventable
World.content:
A coronial inquest has found that a supervised facility for sex offenders in regional Victoria allowed a resident to have control over prescribed medications, which contributed to his death.

A man in his 30s, whose name cannot be published for legal reasons, was serving a post-sentence order at Corella Place, in Ararat, when he was found unresponsive in his unit by staff in May 2020.

Corella Place, managed by Corrections Victoria, is a secure gated complex where former prisoners can live after serving time for sexual offences.

It is not a prison and residents are not serving a custodial sentence but rather live within the parameters of their post-sentence orders as determined by the courts.

Coroner Audrey Jamieson said the deceased was a very vulnerable man and was not at the facility voluntarily.

The report said he had ADHD, depression, anxiety and a history of self-harm episodes.

Ms Jamieson found the man's death was not an intentional act of self-harm, but a result of mixed drug toxicity.

The report said that during the time of the man's death, he was under COVID-19 quarantine, restricted to his unit and a small deck with a balcony for 23 hours a day, with one hour allowed out for exercise.

Corella Place is a residential complex for high-risk sex offenders. (Supplied: Department of Justice and Community Safety)

'Perfect storm' for drug use

An independent expert engaged for the inquiry, clinical forensic medicine and addiction medicine consultant Edward Ogden, said the boredom, isolation and hopelessness inside Corella Place was a "perfect storm" for drug use.

"In [Professor Ogden's] experience treating patients, particularly those on court orders or who had been incarcerated, drug use was often a way to pass the time, and to make life more tolerable," Ms Jamieson said.

"I find that there was a direct link between the failure of Corella Place to properly monitor and control methadone tablets entering the residential facility.

"And I find that Corrections Victoria failed to support [the man] in his rehabilitation."

Ms Jamieson also said the man was not treated with dignity and due respect, given his acquired brain injury and ADHD.

'Failure of Corella Place'

The coroner made 18 recommendations, with 16 directed at the Department of Justice and Community Safety.

Three recommendations were made regarding residents' ability to control their own prescribed medications.

She recommended that patients must disclose when they are prescribed medicines that have the potential for misuse, abuse, and dependence, and that these medications should be administered by staff.

"[And adopt] a system of dispensing medication that replicates the system or systems in place in other correctional facilities known as prisons," she said.

Ms Jamieson also said the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission should review the Department of Justice and Community Safety's training in relation to human rights.

The reports also recommended allowing for more family to visit, and mandatory training to assist residents with disabilities and to recognise signs of drug misuse and overdose.

Corrections Victoria said in a statement to the ABC that it will carefully consider the recommendations.

World.title: Cage fighter was 'mucking around' when spar turned deadly, jury hears
World.content:
A professional cage fighter on trial for murdering his best friend told police he accidentally kicked him in the head while "mucking around" during a sparring session, a Sydney jury has been told.

Bradley Dusan Fletcher was celebrating moving into a rental property in Melonba, near Mount Druitt, with his friend Bradley Evennett one afternoon in March 2024.

The 37-year-old mixed martial arts fighter, who the Crown says "trained religiously to hone his craft", was lightly sparring with Mr Evennett and showing some techniques, and both consumed alcohol and cocaine.

Crown Prosecutor Kate Ratcliffe said that according to Mr Fletcher's girlfriend, the two were drunk but "in a bubbly mood" when she left the property.

"The two mates were having a good time, but things changed," she said during an opening address.

Panicked call to girlfriend

Ms Ratcliffe said the accused "became angry" and deployed his martial arts skills.

"The accused repeatedly struck the deceased to his head and torso, causing the deceased's death."

Mr Evennett, 32, had a genetic condition known as brittle bone disease that was diagnosed when he was 12 years old.

Ms Ratcliffe said Mr Fletcher was aware of that condition and there had been no previous altercations between them.

That evening, Mr Fletcher called his girlfriend and told her Mr Evennett had fallen over and was not breathing.

Jurors heard that she suggested he call an ambulance, but the accused told her to "hurry up and just get here".

A jury heard Mr Fletcher told police he had accidentally kicked his friend in the head while "mucking around". (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

Mr Fletcher's girlfriend is expected to give evidence of seeing blood-staining on the floor around the premises, Mr Evennett lying face down in the backyard and Mr Fletcher pacing.

She left and at some stage, Mr Fletcher used Mr Evennett's car as transport and left his body near a footpath in a nearby street.

After his arrest, the accused told police the two were "sparring".

"I promise you boys it was an accident, man," he said, according to Ms Ratcliffe.

" He's my best friend … I accidentally killed my best friend. Kicked him in the head. "

He referred to being "coked up" and panicking when he realised Mr Evennett had stopped breathing.

Deceased became 'hostile' after blow to ribs

Mr Fletcher also said the deceased "got a bit hostile" after being hit in the ribs.

"I'm a pro cage fighter, I shouldn't be doing that sh*t, you know. I should have called police, whatever, I panicked," he told police.

The jury is expected to hear from a forensic pathologist that the cause of death was multiple blunt force injuries.

That expert was also of the opinion that Mr Evennett's condition, Osteogenesis Imperfecta Type 1, played no real part in his death.

Mr Fletcher pleaded not guilty to murder but guilty to manslaughter. However, the Crown did not accept the manslaughter plea.

Defence counsel James Trevallion SC said Mr Evennett took exception to being hit in the ribs during the sparring and the men removed their boxing gloves and went inside.

But there were further challenges, and they went back outside to continue sparring.

"The hits became more serious. The tensions rose, and the tensions rose for both of them," he said during his opening address.

Mr Trevallion said the sparring was still in the context of the pair being good friends and his client did not intend to really injure Mr Evennett.

He said the primary issue during the trial will be whether Mr Fletcher intended to cause serious injury, which the Crown will be required to prove beyond reasonable doubt.

Mr Trevallion said both men were affected by alcohol and cocaine at the time, urging the jury not to "morally judge them" for their use of the substance.

The Crown will argue that the "extensive" physical assaults would lead jurors to "inevitably conclude" there was an intention to cause serious injury.

"It matters not that he regretted it later," Ms Ratcliffe said.

"That's not the time that you consider his intention. It's at the time of the infliction of the assaults."

Justice Richard Weinstein urged jurors to listen to all of the evidence, the closing addresses and his summing up before making up their minds at the end of the trial, which is expected to last for up to four weeks.

World.title: The first projects to get special treatment under WA’s new state development laws
World.content:
PoliticsWAPlanning and development The first projects to get special treatment under WA’s new state development laws Hamish Hastie April 16, 2026 — 2:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Four wind farms collectively generating more than 1 gigawatt of electricity and a green steel project will be the first major projects to have the red carpet rolled out under the Cook government’s state development laws. WA Premier Roger Cook will announce the first five projects deemed “state priorities” under the controversial State Development Act, which was rushed through parliament at the end of last year, at a Business News breakfast on Thursday morning. The Kwinana industrial area. Cook will also announce that the Western Trade Coast – which incorporates the Kwinana industrial area and Henderson marine precinct – will be declared a state development area under the laws. The four wind farms deemed state priorities include the 470 megawatt Parron Maam Marang Farm near Jurien Bay, the 230 megawatt Kondinin wind farm, the 550 megawatt Marri wind farm in the Shire of Dandaragan, and the 200 megawatt Narrogin wind farm.



The NeoSmelt green iron pilot plant in the Kwinana industrial area, led by steelmaker BlueScope on behalf of a consortium including BHP, Rio Tinto, Woodside Energy and Mitsui Iron Ore, is the only metro non-wind farm project to gain priority project status. Cook said he was putting the State Development Act powers to work. “In designating the first five priority projects and state development area under these new powers, we are delivering on our vision of becoming a renewable energy powerhouse, making more things here and growing the largest naval maintenance and shipbuilding precinct in the southern hemisphere,” he said. The act gives extraordinary powers to the premier and state development minister of the day, allowing them to single out projects they deem crucial for the state and roll out the red carpet for proponents. Once a project is deemed a priority or an industrial zone is declared a special development area, it enlivens powers that help the government of the day streamline approvals through the Office of the Coordinator General.



At the heart of the controversy is a power called a “modification order”, which allows the state development minister of the day to alter aspects of approval processes ascribed in more than 40 pieces of legislation, including environmental approvals, to speed them up. Related Article WA Parliament State development bill vote passes at 3am after marathon debate The Greens’ concerns revolved around the powers it centralised in the premier, state development minister and coordinator general roles, which they said lacked checks and balances and could be abused to ram through projects that were bad for the environment. However, industry backed the laws, saying they would help reduce lengthy approval delays and improve investment attractiveness in the state. The government spruiked the laws as crucial to it achieving its goal of getting out of coal-fired power by 2030 by fast-tracking renewable projects.



Energy and Decarbonisation; Manufacturing Minister Amber Jade Sanderson was buoyant that four of the first five priority projects were onshore wind farms. “Together, these wind farms will unlock more than one gigawatt of renewable energy, helping us to get out of coal by 2030 and secure clean, affordable and reliable power for the future,” she said. “This is a crucial step towards getting out of coal by 2030 and developing WA as a global renewable energy powerhouse. “By fast-tracking these projects, we’re creating a stronger future for WA, diversifying the economy and creating great local jobs.” The Cook government reconvened parliament in mid-December to pass the act, with Cook citing the need to have the laws in place as soon as possible so priority projects could be declared as soon as possible.



This announcement comes nearly three months after parliament returned from the Christmas break. Since the bill passed, the state has been drafting the Coordinator General guidelines. The government has also announced more than $90 million as part of the 2026-27 budget to boost industrial land across the state, including $45.2 million for land acquisition at the Latitude 32 estate in the western trade coast zone. World.title: $53 billion to be ploughed into Australia’s defence budget. Trump’s secretary of war wanted more
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDefence $53 billion to be ploughed into Australia’s defence budget. Trump’s secretary of war wanted more Matthew Knott April 15, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

An extra $53 billion will be injected into defence over the next 10 years as the Albanese government seeks to rebuff claims the nation’s military is dangerously unprepared for the age of modern warfare. The government will argue defence spending will grow to 3 per cent of gross domestic product by 2033 – the level demanded by a raft of military experts – but only by junking the definition traditionally used in Australia to calculate this influential figure. Even using the new method to calculate defence funding, the figure falls short of the 3.5 per cent of GDP target that Trump’s Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has called for Australia to spend on defence. Defence Minister Richard Marles said the government was making the biggest ever peacetime increase in defence spending. Oscar Colman The budget boost, which includes an extra $14 billion for defence over the next four years, is a win for Defence Minister Richard Marles and Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy, who have argued within cabinet that a significant increase is needed for a tumultuous era in which countries are increasingly using force, rather than diplomacy, to resolve disputes.



Many defence experts and the Coalition, however, are likely to argue that the increase still falls short of the funding level needed to ensure Australia can pay for the AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine program without draining the rest of the defence force. The extra defence spending, which amounts to around a 5 per cent increase over the next four years, comes on top of $50 billion in additional defence funding over a decade announced by the government in 2024. The government has flagged it will need to cut, cancel and delay some planned defence programs to pay for extra spending on drones and other advanced technologies, though it has not yet revealed its targets. Defence Minister Richard Marles will tell the National Press Club on Thursday that the government was making “the biggest peacetime increase in defence spending in our nation’s history”. “International norms that once constrained the use of force and military coercion continue to erode,” Marles will say, according to speech notes.



“More countries are engaged in conflict today than at any time since the end of World War II, and this is occurring across every region of the world.” Related Article Defence ‘The threat is here now’: Australia dangerously exposed without rise in defence spending Marles will say the new defence strategy is “not a departure in direction, but a strengthening of resolve with an increased focus on self-reliance”. The government is seeking to tap alternative forms of defence funding, including equity-based financing through government agencies, and private sector investment, Marles will say. Speaking before the release of the new defence strategy, former defence department boss Dennis Richardson said: “If you maintain all the existing capability that we have and, in addition, have nuclear-powered submarines, you’re going to spend more than 3 per cent of GDP on defence.



“Anyone who argues differently is seeking to pull the wool over people’s eyes.” Australia spends around 2 per cent of GDP on defence, a figure that was set to rise to 2.33 per cent by 2033 under the funding plan announced two years ago. The government will claim defence spending will hit 3 per cent of GDP by 2033 by using a North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) definition that differs from Australia’s traditional calculation by including money spent on military pensions and a broader definition of military infrastructure. Marles argued last year that Australia was already spending 2.8 per cent of GDP on defence using the NATO definition, reflecting the significant discrepancy between the two methods. The opposition, which went to the last election promising to raise defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP, is likely to accuse the government of using accounting trickery to claim a major increase in defence spending when it is not dramatically rising as a proportion of GDP.



The funding details were provided to journalists on the condition they not seek comment from third parties. Speaking ahead of the release of the figures, retired major-general Mick Ryan said he feared the ADF was becoming too focused on naval capabilities such as frigates and submarines as he argued the army and air force should not be marginalised. Related Article Middle East at war Australia joins strait-talking summit with France and UK, and without the US “The threat is here now, and we need to be spending big by the end of the decade to help prevent an even more catastrophic situation in our region than we have seen in Ukraine and Iran,” he said. Ian Langford, a retired senior army officer who served in top roles in the ADF, said: “The government’s rhetoric about Australia facing its most dangerous security circumstance since the Second World War is not being matched by resources.”



Langford said increased investment in air defence technology to protect the nation, and key military assets, from drone and missile attacks should be a top priority for the new spending plan. He acknowledged the government may find it difficult to acquire weapons and equipment from the United States and other suppliers after they have been depleted by the war in Iran. The government announced this week that it would spend between $2 billion and $5 billion more over 10 years on uncrewed systems such as drones than previously forecast. The defence establishment is also being shaken up, with navy chief Mark Hammond to take over as defence force chief and Susan Coyle promoted to be the nation’s first female head of army. Two popular inner-city parks will be partially closed after testing revealed potentially toxic heavy metals in the soil.

Brisbane City Council confirmed substances including copper, nickel and zinc had been detected at James Warner Park and C.T. White Park on the west side of Kangaroo Point.

“[These] are really special riverside spaces with a long history,” Tracy Davis, chair of the council’s environment, parks and sustainability committee, said in a statement.

C.T. White Park at Kangaroo Point is one of two parks to partially close. William Davis

“After undergoing testing and determining the best approach, we’re getting on with cleaning up the parks so they can be enjoyed by residents for years to come.”

World.title: $53 billion to be ploughed into Australia’s defence budget. Trump’s secretary of war wanted more
World.content:
PoliticsFederalDefence $53 billion to be ploughed into Australia’s defence budget. Trump’s secretary of war wanted more Matthew Knott April 15, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

An extra $53 billion will be injected into defence over the next 10 years as the Albanese government seeks to rebuff claims the nation’s military is dangerously unprepared for the age of modern warfare. The government will argue defence spending will grow to 3 per cent of gross domestic product by 2033 – the level demanded by a raft of military experts – but only by junking the definition traditionally used in Australia to calculate this influential figure. Even using the new method to calculate defence funding, the figure falls short of the 3.5 per cent of GDP target that Trump’s Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has called for Australia to spend on defence. Defence Minister Richard Marles said the government was making the biggest ever peacetime increase in defence spending. Oscar Colman The budget boost, which includes an extra $14 billion for defence over the next four years, is a win for Defence Minister Richard Marles and Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy, who have argued within cabinet that a significant increase is needed for a tumultuous era in which countries are increasingly using force, rather than diplomacy, to resolve disputes.



Many defence experts and the Coalition, however, are likely to argue that the increase still falls short of the funding level needed to ensure Australia can pay for the AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine program without draining the rest of the defence force. The extra defence spending, which amounts to around a 5 per cent increase over the next four years, comes on top of $50 billion in additional defence funding over a decade announced by the government in 2024. The government has flagged it will need to cut, cancel and delay some planned defence programs to pay for extra spending on drones and other advanced technologies, though it has not yet revealed its targets. Defence Minister Richard Marles will tell the National Press Club on Thursday that the government was making “the biggest peacetime increase in defence spending in our nation’s history”. “International norms that once constrained the use of force and military coercion continue to erode,” Marles will say, according to speech notes.



“More countries are engaged in conflict today than at any time since the end of World War II, and this is occurring across every region of the world.” Related Article Defence ‘The threat is here now’: Australia dangerously exposed without rise in defence spending Marles will say the new defence strategy is “not a departure in direction, but a strengthening of resolve with an increased focus on self-reliance”. The government is seeking to tap alternative forms of defence funding, including equity-based financing through government agencies, and private sector investment, Marles will say. Speaking before the release of the new defence strategy, former defence department boss Dennis Richardson said: “If you maintain all the existing capability that we have and, in addition, have nuclear-powered submarines, you’re going to spend more than 3 per cent of GDP on defence.



“Anyone who argues differently is seeking to pull the wool over people’s eyes.” Australia spends around 2 per cent of GDP on defence, a figure that was set to rise to 2.33 per cent by 2033 under the funding plan announced two years ago. The government will claim defence spending will hit 3 per cent of GDP by 2033 by using a North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) definition that differs from Australia’s traditional calculation by including money spent on military pensions and a broader definition of military infrastructure. Marles argued last year that Australia was already spending 2.8 per cent of GDP on defence using the NATO definition, reflecting the significant discrepancy between the two methods. The opposition, which went to the last election promising to raise defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP, is likely to accuse the government of using accounting trickery to claim a major increase in defence spending when it is not dramatically rising as a proportion of GDP.



The funding details were provided to journalists on the condition they not seek comment from third parties. Speaking ahead of the release of the figures, retired major-general Mick Ryan said he feared the ADF was becoming too focused on naval capabilities such as frigates and submarines as he argued the army and air force should not be marginalised. Related Article Middle East at war Australia joins strait-talking summit with France and UK, and without the US “The threat is here now, and we need to be spending big by the end of the decade to help prevent an even more catastrophic situation in our region than we have seen in Ukraine and Iran,” he said. Ian Langford, a retired senior army officer who served in top roles in the ADF, said: “The government’s rhetoric about Australia facing its most dangerous security circumstance since the Second World War is not being matched by resources.”



Langford said increased investment in air defence technology to protect the nation, and key military assets, from drone and missile attacks should be a top priority for the new spending plan. He acknowledged the government may find it difficult to acquire weapons and equipment from the United States and other suppliers after they have been depleted by the war in Iran. The government announced this week that it would spend between $2 billion and $5 billion more over 10 years on uncrewed systems such as drones than previously forecast. The defence establishment is also being shaken up, with navy chief Mark Hammond to take over as defence force chief and Susan Coyle promoted to be the nation’s first female head of army. Two popular inner-city parks will be partially closed after testing revealed potentially toxic heavy metals in the soil.

Brisbane City Council confirmed substances including copper, nickel and zinc had been detected at James Warner Park and C.T. White Park on the west side of Kangaroo Point.

“[These] are really special riverside spaces with a long history,” Tracy Davis, chair of the council’s environment, parks and sustainability committee, said in a statement.

C.T. White Park at Kangaroo Point is one of two parks to partially close. William Davis

“After undergoing testing and determining the best approach, we’re getting on with cleaning up the parks so they can be enjoyed by residents for years to come.”
